notes:
I've organised these notes by verse. The commentary notes for vv. 27–53 come mostly from older works collected on biblehub.com and studylight.org (Gill, Clarke, Henry, Barnes, Poole, Benson, Ellicott, Pulpit, Keil & Delitzsch, Cambridge Bible) and from Enduring Word.

**What I couldn't find:**
- **Tradition-by-tradition views:** I didn't find any denominational site (Ligonier, Desiring God, Seedbed, LCMS, etc.) discussing these verses. Where the commentators below disagree, I've noted the disagreement, but I haven't labelled anyone by tradition, because the pages don't say which tradition each writer belongs to.
- **Other views:** I found nothing from Catholic or Orthodox sites, bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes, or prosperity/word-of-faith/hyper-grace teaching. The only "other views" are the Septuagint, Josephus and rabbinic readings that the older commentaries mention.
- **Precept Austin:** its 1 Kings 22 page cut off before v. 27, so I could only use a few short excerpts from it.

---

**v. 27:** Ahab reacts like a tyrant faced with the truth. He wants Micaiah locked up and kept short of food. Dilday says "bread of affliction and water of affliction" can mean bread and water in small amounts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/
- Matthew Henry: the prophet was in chains, but God's word was not. Prison didn't weaken his courage or his faithfulness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_022.cfm
- Precept Austin: Micaiah was better off as a prophet on bread and water than as a guest at Ahab's feasts. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-22-commentary

**v. 28:** Micaiah makes a last appeal. He is willing to be judged by whether his prophecy comes true. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/

**v. 29:** Guzik says Ahab's going is easy to understand: he refused to believe the prophecy and wanted to defy it. Jehoshaphat's going is harder to explain, since he should have believed Micaiah. Guzik suggests Jehoshaphat may have taken a fatalistic view of God's will. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/
- Henry: Ahab going on is not strange, but it is "astonishing" that the godly Jehoshaphat went on after such a clear warning. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_022.cfm

**v. 30:**
- **Guzik:** Ahab didn't want to stand out as a king and become a special target. He thought a disguise would protect him from Micaiah's prophecy. Why Jehoshaphat agreed to be the only recognisable king is unclear: either he wasn't very wise or he had great faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/
- **Clarke:** he rejects the rabbi Jarchi's idea that Ahab meant "the Syrians won't bother you." If Jehoshaphat was helping Ahab, the Syrians would hardly spare him. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-kings-22.html
- **Henry (Concise):** Ahab meanly planned to expose Jehoshaphat to danger to keep himself safe. That is what comes of joining with wicked men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-38.htm

**v. 31:**
- **Guzik:** Ahab's earlier mercy to Ben-hadad won him no lasting goodwill. The Syrian order made Ahab's disguise look wise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/
- **Henry:** Ben-hadad had no quarrel with Judah. Ahab was rightly paid back for sparing Ben-hadad, who stung the hand that had saved him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_022.cfm

**vv. 32–33:**
- **Henry:** the danger showed that God was displeased with Jehoshaphat's alliance. Jehoshaphat had told Ahab "I am as you are" (v. 4), and now he was actually mistaken for him. The rescue showed that God had not abandoned him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_022.cfm
- **Guzik:** Jehoshaphat cried out to the LORD and was rescued, and later recommitted himself to reform in Judah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/

**v. 34:**
- **Providence (the common reading):** Guzik says the shot looked like pure chance, but God used a man's unintended action to carry out His judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/
- Henry says no armour protects against God's judgment. What looks like chance comes from God's settled plan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-34.htm
- A Bible Hub study note links the verse to Proverbs 16:33. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/22-34.htm
- **The Hebrew phrase:**
  - Poole: it literally means "in his simplicity," meaning the archer didn't know he was aiming at Ahab. Poole also mentions another possible meaning: "with his full strength." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-34.htm
  - Cambridge Bible: the archer was aiming at some enemy without knowing who it was, so the phrase shouldn't be read as "a shot at random." Barnes: "without intent to kill the king." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-34.htm
- **Who was the archer?** Josephus names him Aman, a relative of Ben-hadad, and some rabbis identified him with Naaman. The Cambridge Bible says naming him goes against the spirit of the story. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-34.htm
- **Translations differ:** the Septuagint (Brenton) says he shot "with a good aim," and the Douay-Rheims says the arrow struck "between the lungs and the stomach." https://biblehub.com/parallel/1_kings/22-34.htm
- **The armour:** Barnes says the "joints" were probably pieces linking the breastplate to other parts of the armour, and the arrow went in between them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-34.htm

**v. 35:**
- Guzik: Ahab met death bravely, propped up in his chariot to encourage his troops. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/
- Constable: Ahab couldn't fool or beat God. One arrow, guided by providence, was all it took. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-35.html

**v. 36:** Guzik quotes Clarke: once the king's death became known, a proclamation probably ended the battle, perhaps with both sides agreeing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/

**v. 37:**
- Coffman, quoting the Wycliffe commentary: Jezebel was to be eaten by dogs, but Ahab's temporary repentance won him an honourable burial. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-38.html
- Constable: that Ahab was buried at all shows God's grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-38.html

**v. 38:** This is the most debated verse.
- **Was Elijah's prophecy (21:19) fulfilled exactly?** The commentators disagree:
  - **Guzik:** it was "almost" fulfilled, true but not in the place Elijah named. God softened the first sentence, but because Ahab's repentance was false and he kept sinning, a very similar judgment came. Guzik also sees 1 Kings 20:42 fulfilled here. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/
  - **Keil & Delitzsch:** because Ahab humbled himself, the threat was only partly fulfilled in him. It was fulfilled literally in his son Joram (2 Kings 9:25–26). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/21-19.html
  - **Coffman:** Jezreel and Samaria were both in the one kingdom of Samaria and less than seven miles apart, so the prophecy was fulfilled. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-38.html
  - **Gill:** it was fulfilled, though not in the same place, and the same place wasn't required. Some read 21:19 as "because" rather than "in the place where." He also mentions a theory that the blood flowed down to Jezreel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-38.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/21-19.html
  - **Cambridge Bible:** it happened in the same kind of place, outside the city walls. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-38.htm
  - **Josephus:** he puts the washing at the "fountain of Jezreel." The Pulpit Commentary thinks this change was made to avoid the discrepancy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-38.htm
- **"Washed his armour" (KJV) or "the harlots bathed"?**
  - Ellicott, the Cambridge Bible and Barnes follow the Septuagint and Josephus: prostitutes bathed in the pool. The Cambridge Bible says the KJV reading comes from the Aramaic and Syriac versions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-38.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch say the grammar shows the prostitutes were bathing while the chariot was washed, a sign of the contempt heaped on Ahab at his death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-38.htm
  - Gill mentions an odd tradition that Jezebel had two prostitutes painted on the chariot. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-38.htm
- **Were these temple prostitutes?** The Expositor's Bible Commentary (in Spanish on StudyLight) takes them as devotees of Asherah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-40.html The Cambridge Bible rejects this as reading too much into the text. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-38.htm
- **Lessons drawn:**
  - Ellicott: the dog and the harlot are the animal and human pictures of uncleanness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-38.htm
  - Constable: the place was fitting, because Ahab too had "sold himself." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-38.html
  - Henry: Naboth's blood was avenged, and Psalm 68:23 was fulfilled. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-37.html
- **Septuagint addition:** it adds "swine." Gill thinks this unlikely, since pigs weren't raised in Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-38.html

**v. 39:** Guzik: by material standards Ahab's reign succeeded, with military wins and a generally prosperous economy. Spiritually it was one of Israel's worst. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/

**v. 40:** Guzik: Ahaziah reigned only two years before judgment fell, as prophesied. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/

**vv. 41–42:** GotQuestions (quoted on Precept Austin) dates Jehoshaphat's reign to 873–848 BC. It notes that 2 Chronicles 17–22 tells his story more fully. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-22-commentary

**v. 43:** How does this fit with 2 Chronicles 17:6, which says Jehoshaphat *did* remove the high places? Several explanations are offered:
- **Clarke:** there were two kinds of high places, idolatrous ones (which he removed) and ones dedicated to God (which he left). Some think the Chronicles text is corrupt and originally said "he did *not* take away." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-43.html
- **Barnes:** Chronicles describes what the king wanted and intended; Kings records that his efforts failed in practice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-43.html
- **Constable:** he removed them early in his reign, then let them stand once the people rebuilt them (2 Chronicles 20:33). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-43.html
- **Gill:** he removed the idolatrous ones but not those where sacrifices were offered to the LORD, which he should also have removed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-43.html
- **Bible Hub Q&A:** it combines these. The reforms were real but partial, some sites came back, and the problem lay in the people's hearts. https://biblehub.com/q/why_the_discrepancy_on_jehoshaphat's_actions.htm
- **Guzik:** Jehoshaphat didn't do everything he should have. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/

**v. 44:**
- Coffman: calling Jehoshaphat "right" is not a blanket approval. His peace with Ahab is singled out as a fault. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-43.html
- Henry: his close ties to Ahab's family were the one thing that tarnished his greatness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-43.html
- Wiersbe (on Precept Austin): Jehoshaphat disobeyed the Lord in this, and one compromise leads to another. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-22-commentary

**v. 46:**
- Clarke: the Hebrew means "consecrated persons." It may refer to the whole system of debauched worship of Baal and Ashtaroth. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-kings-22.html
- Guzik: in this, Jehoshaphat reformed more deeply than Asa. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-22/

**v. 47:**
- Clarke: this shows the book's compiler lived after Jehoshaphat, when Edom revolted (2 Kings 8:22). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-kings-22.html
- Coffman, citing the Pulpit Commentary: the deputy was appointed by Jehoshaphat, which explains how he could build a fleet at Ezion-geber. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-49.html

**v. 48:**
- **"Ships of Tarshish":** Benson says this means ships built on the Tarshish model, not ships headed for Tarshish. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-48.htm
- **The fuller story in 2 Chronicles 20:35–37:** Ellicott says it was a joint fleet with Israel, condemned by the prophet Eliezer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-48.htm
- **What wrecked the ships?**
  - Benson and Keil: probably a storm. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-48.htm
  - Coffman: some blame incompetent sailors, but it could have been a storm or a fire. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-49.html
  - Constable: possibly the Edomites. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-49.html
- **Its meaning:** a Bible Hub study note calls the wreck God's judgment on an unequal alliance. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/22-48.htm Guzik sees it as God's mercy, keeping Jehoshaphat from making the mistake worse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-20/

**v. 49:** How does this fit with Chronicles, where Jehoshaphat *did* join Ahaziah?
- **Clarke:** perhaps this refers to a second voyage. Some critics would even read "Jehoshaphat consented." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/22-49.html
- **Pulpit:** he refused because of Eliezer's prophecy and the wreck, not mainly because Ahaziah's offer implied his sailors were unskilled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-49.htm
- **Benson:** the refusal showed that his repentance was sincere. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-49.htm
- **Cambridge Bible:** there may have been two planned voyages, one to Ophir and one to Tarshish. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/22-49.htm

**v. 50:** Utley (on Precept Austin): Jehoshaphat's son Joram (Jehoram) married Ahab's daughter Athaliah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-22-commentary

**vv. 51–53:**
- Henry: Ahaziah kept up Jeroboam's idolatry and Baal worship as well. He learned nothing from his father's ruin and followed his mother Jezebel, who was still alive. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_022.cfm
- Precept Austin: Elijah later repeated God's judgment to Ahaziah, who soon died (2 Kings 1). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-22-commentary

I found nothing specific on v. 45.
